questions.question: A dense-model training run triples its GPU count from 64 to 192 while holding the global work per update fixed. Step time drops by only 30%, and per-GPU compute utilization falls. Which scaling mechanism should the team investigate, without treating these aggregates as proof of the cause?
choices: Backpropagation stops functioning correctly across multiple nodes because gradients cannot be computed concurrently across independent data batches.
Floating-point accumulation during gradient reduction becomes numerically unstable when more than 64 GPUs participate in the collective.
Host CPU memory bandwidth saturates because all optimizer states must be shuffled through host DRAM on every multi-node step.
Local compute can shrink while global synchronization and shared-link transfers remain exposed; rank-aligned traces are needed to determine whether communication actually limits the step.
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. Under fixed global work, added workers can reduce local computation while required exchanges retain startup, byte-transfer, and coordination costs. Those costs may then occupy more of the critical path. Step time and utilization alone do not identify communication as the cause: input stalls, placement, kernel efficiency, or stragglers can produce similar symptoms. Compare rank-aligned readiness and transfer traces with matched collective measurements before selecting an intervention.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze why per-GPU compute utilization drops as distributed training scales using the local-compute versus global-communication asymmetry.

questions.question: A machine learning engineer evaluates the communication traffic induced by different model parallelism strategies. According to the chapter travel manifest, which mapping correctly pairs a parallelism strategy with its primary collective primitive and primary physical constraint?
choices: Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) -> Broadcast primitive -> Memory capacity constraint.
Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Routing -> AllToAll primitive -> Latency and bisection network contention constraint.
Tensor Parallelism within a node -> Point-to-Point Send/Recv -> Inter-node bisection bandwidth constraint.
Data Parallelism -> Reduce primitive -> Host-to-device PCIe bandwidth constraint.
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. MoE routing exchanges token payloads with the ranks hosting selected experts. Its all-to-all pattern can create many peer messages, skewed destinations, and bisection contention. The $N(N-1)$ potential directed peer relationships do not imply quadratic bytes at fixed per-rank payload. FSDP uses AllGather and ReduceScatter, while dense data-parallel training uses AllReduce rather than root-only Reduce.
questions.learning_objective: Classify distributed parallelism strategies by their corresponding collective communication primitives and governing physical constraints.

questions.question: A logical Ring AllReduce cost model uses a 140 GB input per rank, corresponding to the model-wide BF16 gradient size of a 70B-parameter model. Holding that input fixed, a team expects per-rank sent volume to grow over 100 times when the group grows from 8 to 1,000 ranks. Explain why the expectation is false and why time can still increase. Treat this as transfer arithmetic, not a claim that a full replicated training state fits on one GPU.
questions.answer: The expectation is false because Ring AllReduce decouples per-node byte volume from cluster size: each participant transfers exactly $2 \cdot \frac{N-1}{N} \cdot M$ bytes sent, and the same volume received, across the scatter-reduce and all-gather phases. For $N=8$, each GPU transfers $2 \cdot (7/8) \cdot 140\text{ GB} = 245\text{ GB}$; for $N=1{,}000$, each GPU transfers $2 \cdot (999/1000) \cdot 140\text{ GB} = 279.72\text{ GB}$, an increase of only 14%, approaching the asymptotic $2M = 280\text{ GB}$ ceiling. What actually causes synchronization time to increase at large scale is not per-node volume, but: (1) the linear growth in sequential latency hops ($2(N-1)\alpha$), which adds barrier overhead; (2) the physical transition from high-bandwidth intra-node NVLink (450 GB/s one-way) to lower-bandwidth inter-node InfiniBand (50 GB/s per port); and (3) network switch hops and straggler delays that amplify across thousands of participants.
questions.learning_objective: Calculate per-node Ring AllReduce communication volume and identify the physical mechanisms that increase synchronization overhead at large scale.

questions.question: True or False: In synchronous data-parallel distributed training, using Ring AllReduce causes each GPU network bandwidth requirement to scale quadratically with the number of GPUs $N$ because every worker must open a direct communication socket to every other worker in the cluster.
questions.answer: False. A ring exchanges chunks with neighbors. Each rank sends $2(N-1)M/N$ bytes and receives the same amount; this approaches $2M$ in each direction. AllToAll has $N(N-1)$ directed peer relationships, but quadratic peer count does not imply quadratic bytes or bisection demand when the total per-rank payload is fixed.
questions.learning_objective: Distinguish the linear ring neighbor topology of Ring AllReduce from the quadratic connection pattern of AllToAll.

questions.question: On a supported hardware and transport path, the mechanism that lets a NIC read and write GPU memory without staging payloads through host DRAM is known as ____ RDMA.
questions.answer: GPUDirect. A supported GPUDirect RDMA path lets the NIC access GPU memory without staging the payload through host DRAM. This removes that staging traffic, but does not guarantee a particular launch latency, eliminate CPU coordination, or prevent every source of host-memory contention. Measure the configured device, PCIe, NIC, and transport path.
questions.learning_objective: Identify GPUDirect RDMA as a mechanism for avoiding host-memory payload staging.

questions.question: A single-transfer model uses effective startup cost $\alpha=1.5\,\mu\text{s}$ and per-direction bandwidth $\beta=50\text{ GB/s}$. Which conclusion follows for a 4 KB transfer, and what must be added before classifying a complete gradient AllReduce?
choices: The single-transfer knee is 75 KB, so startup dominates the 4 KB transfer. A complete AllReduce additionally requires the schedule’s round count and chunk size, then calibration for its placement.
The 4 KB transfer is bandwidth-bound because adding ranks makes every individual transfer saturate its port.
The 75 KB knee is a maximum buffer size, so larger messages cannot be sent over this link.
The critical message size defines the maximum possible buffer size that can be transferred in a single CUDA stream without host CPU intervention.
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. The single-transfer terms are equal at $\alpha\beta=75\text{ KB}$. A 4 KB transfer therefore spends more modeled time in startup than in byte transfer. Fusion of compatible ready messages or a lower-overhead path are candidates, with packing and readiness costs included. For a ring AllReduce of an $M$-byte tensor over $N$ ranks, compare each $M/N$ chunk with the knee and count $2(N-1)$ rounds; the full tensor’s size alone does not classify the schedule. Compression only removes byte-transfer work and must also win against encoding, aggregation, and quality costs.
questions.learning_objective: Apply the critical message size $n^* = \alpha \cdot \beta$ to classify communication workloads into latency-bound and bandwidth-bound regimes.

questions.question: In a toy overlap budget, independent computation takes $600\,\mu\text{s}$ and the complete network interval takes $200\,\mu\text{s}$. Initiation and completion each cost $50\,\mu\text{s}$ on the same execution resource as that computation. Assume independent network progress and no contention. What is the effective elapsed time, and which component remains exposed?
choices: Effective time is $600\,\mu\text{s}$, and communication is 100% hidden because $L_{\text{lat}} < T_{\text{compute}}$.
Effective time is $800\,\mu\text{s}$, because network latency and processor overhead must both be added directly to compute time.
Effective time is $750\,\mu\text{s}$, because the gap parameter $g$ adds an irreducible stall to the compute pipeline.

Effective time is $700\,\mu\text{s}$ ($2o + \max(T_{\text{compute}}, L_{\text{lat}})$), where the $200\,\mu\text{s}$ network latency is completely hidden behind the $600\,\mu\text{s}$ compute, but the $100\,\mu\text{s}$ of processor overhead ($2o$) remains exposed.
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. Under the stated shared-resource assumptions, initiation and completion add $2o=100\,\mu\text{s}$. Independent computation hides the 200-microsecond network interval, giving $2o+\max(600,200)=700\,\mu\text{s}$. This is a scoped overlap budget, not a claim that all CPU coordination blocks every GPU execution resource. Other processor placement, dependencies, progress, or contention require a different schedule.
questions.learning_objective: Calculate effective overlapped step time using the LogP model by separating overlappable wire latency from nonoverlappable processor overhead.

questions.question: Explain why small-message collective timings can exceed a bare-wire prediction by a much larger relative factor than large-message timings. Which measurements are needed before using this difference in a cluster capacity plan?
questions.answer: Small transfers can spend most of their time in launch, descriptor preparation, registration, proxy processing, and synchronization rather than serialization. For large transfers, the payload-over-bandwidth term can dominate those fixed costs. Benchmark effective startup latency and sustained bandwidth for the intended message sizes, placement, and concurrent traffic. The discrepancy is configuration-dependent, so an illustrative overhead ratio is not a measured hardware guarantee.
questions.learning_objective: Explain the NCCL reality gap by contrasting software stack launch overheads in small messages with wire saturation in large payloads.

questions.question: True or False: In the stated toy LogP budget with independent work, network progress, and no contention, upgrading a network fabric to achieve lower physical wire latency ($L_{\text{lat}}$) will not reduce step time if the overlapped computation window $T_{\text{compute}}$ already exceeds $L_{\text{lat}}$ and the nonoverlappable processor overhead $o$ remains unchanged.
questions.answer: True under those assumptions. The budget is $2o+\max(T_{\text{compute}},L_{\text{lat}})$. When independent compute already covers the complete network interval, reducing that interval alone leaves the maximum and elapsed time unchanged. This does not establish the same result for a different dependency schedule, processor placement, or contended transfer.
questions.learning_objective: Evaluate how computation-latency overlap renders further wire latency reductions ineffective when processor overhead dominates.

questions.question: Sequence the hierarchy of communication cost models and diagnostic analyses in order from the simplest zero-overlap first-order sizing to real-world cluster validation: (1) empirically benchmark bare collectives with nccl-tests to capture cluster-specific reality gaps and contention, (2) compute critical message size $n^* = \alpha \cdot \beta$ using the $\alpha$-$\beta$ model to classify latency vs bandwidth regimes, (3) profile processor overhead $o$ and overlappable latency $L_{\text{lat}}$ using the LogP model to assess overlap feasibility with the backward pass.
questions.answer: The correct order is: (2) compute critical message size $n^* = \alpha \cdot \beta$ using the $\alpha$-$\beta$ model to classify latency vs bandwidth regimes, (3) profile processor overhead $o$ and overlappable latency $L_{\text{lat}}$ using the LogP model to assess overlap feasibility with the backward pass, (1) empirically benchmark bare collectives with nccl-tests to capture cluster-specific reality gaps and contention. Engineers start with the analytical $\alpha$-$\beta$ model for initial sizing and regime classification; refine with the LogP model when designing compute-communication overlap to distinguish nonoverlappable processor overhead from overlappable wire transit; and finally validate against actual cluster behavior using bare collective benchmarks (`nccl-tests`) to expose hardware topology, network contention, and software runtime overheads.
questions.learning_objective: Order the progression of communication modeling techniques from analytical sizing to empirical cluster benchmarking.

questions.question: Why can MoE token routing with AllToAll encounter contention and tail-latency limits even when its per-worker payload is smaller than that of a dense AllReduce?
choices: AllToAll transfers more total bytes per GPU than AllReduce, requiring each GPU to send $2(N-1)M$ bytes instead of $2 \frac{N-1}{N} M$ bytes.
AllToAll exchanges distinct payloads among many peers; routing skew and concurrent cross-fabric transfers can concentrate traffic on shared links and destinations.
AllToAll cannot execute over InfiniBand fabrics and must fall back to host CPU TCP/IP socket emulation.
AllToAll mandates single-precision FP32 representation, preventing BF16 or FP16 tensor transfers across remote experts.
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. AllToAll has $N(N-1)$ potential directed peer relationships, so placement, routing, and load imbalance matter as well as total bytes. With a fixed total $M$-byte input per rank, uniform AllToAll sends $(N-1)M/N$ bytes per rank, not a quadratic volume. Traffic can still contend on a limited bisection or overloaded expert. The operation does not inherently require TCP or FP32.
questions.learning_objective: Compare the scaling constraints of AllToAll and AllReduce by analyzing logical connection density and network bisection contention.

questions.question: How does the communication pattern of Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP / ZeRO-3) differ structurally and operationally from standard Distributed Data Parallelism (DDP)?
choices: DDP communicates twice per transformer layer using Point-to-Point Send/Recv, whereas FSDP communicates only once at the end of the step using Broadcast.
FSDP replaces all network communication with CPU host memory paging, eliminating collective communication entirely.

DDP reduces ready gradient buckets, whereas layer-wrapped full-shard FSDP with resharding typically issues $3N_L$ collectives: forward and backward AllGathers plus backward ReduceScatters, increasing launch-latency sensitivity.
FSDP eliminates AllGather operations by permanently keeping full model parameters in every GPU high-bandwidth memory.
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. DDP keeps replicated state and launches AllReduce as gradient buckets become ready. With one FSDP unit per layer and resharding after forward, two AllGathers and one ReduceScatter produce approximately $3N_L$ calls per step. Wrapping and resharding policy can change that count. FSDP saves resident state through communication, not by eliminating networking or permanently retaining full parameters.
questions.learning_objective: Contrast the communication frequency, message granularity, and latency sensitivity of FSDP with standard Data Parallelism.

questions.question: In Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP), when does a parameter AllGather or gradient ReduceScatter add exposed delay to a training step? Explain why the primitive name alone does not identify a latency-bound or bandwidth-bound transfer.
questions.answer: A layer waits when its parameter AllGather has not completed by the time computation needs those parameters. Prefetching can hide the gather within independent work, at the cost of additional resident parameters. ReduceScatter starts after the required gradients are ready and can overlap remaining backward computation, but its final transfer or backlog can remain exposed before the optimizer step. Message size, group size, topology, achieved transfer duration, and the available overlap window determine the cost; a consumer dependency does not establish startup dominance.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze FSDP communication exposure using parameter dependencies, gradient readiness, prefetch memory, and available overlap windows.

questions.question: True or False: In a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model where tokens are routed across 8 GPUs using full-duplex InfiniBand NDR (50 GB/s per port), issuing 7 concurrent peer transfers allows the GPU to achieve an aggregate outgoing transmission rate of $7 \times 50\text{ GB/s} = 350\text{ GB/s}$.
questions.answer: False. Full-duplex communication allows a network interface card (NIC) to send and receive simultaneously at line rate (50 GB/s in each direction), but it does not multiply the physical injection bandwidth of a single port across multiple concurrent destinations. All concurrent outgoing peer streams share the same physical 50 GB/s injection link, meaning total outgoing data must serialize through that single port. The aggregate outgoing transmission rate remains bounded by the 50 GB/s link capacity.
questions.learning_objective: Distinguish full-duplex bidirectional link capability from multi-destination injection bandwidth limits.

questions.question: The mathematical identity that an AllReduce can be decomposed into an intra-group ____ phase (where each worker retains a reduced chunk) followed by an ____ phase (where workers circulate and concatenate the reduced chunks) forms the foundational communication mechanism behind both Ring AllReduce and ZeRO-3/FSDP memory sharding.
questions.answer: ReduceScatter, AllGather (or Reduce-Scatter and All-Gather). In Ring AllReduce, this decomposition executes in two $N-1$ step phases; in FSDP, the AllGather is invoked per layer during the forward pass to reconstruct parameters, and the ReduceScatter is invoked during the backward pass to shard the accumulated gradients.
questions.learning_objective: Identify the fundamental two-phase decomposition of AllReduce into ReduceScatter and AllGather.

questions.question: Why does Ring AllReduce achieve the information-theoretic lower bound for bandwidth ($2 \frac{N-1}{N} \frac{M}{\beta}$) while a simple unsegmented binary Tree AllReduce incurs a bandwidth penalty of $\mathcal{O}(\log N \cdot \frac{M}{\beta})$?
choices: Ring AllReduce distributes uniform chunks ($M/N$) across all logical ring edges in each round, whereas the simple unsegmented tree sends full messages through successive levels of a reduction and broadcast.
Ring AllReduce compresses floating-point gradients to 1-bit representations during ring circulation, whereas Tree AllReduce always uses uncompressed FP64 precision.
Tree AllReduce requires an external parameter server node to perform floating-point additions, whereas Ring AllReduce computes sums purely in network switch ASICs.
Ring AllReduce eliminates the latency term $\alpha$ entirely by using asynchronous token rings, whereas Tree AllReduce scales latency quadratically with cluster size.
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. Each ring rank sends a uniform chunk in every round, yielding the balanced byte-volume lower bound. The simple unsegmented tree instead forwards full messages along successive levels, adding byte-transfer time to the dependency path. Logical ring edges may share physical links, so byte optimality does not guarantee peak link utilization. The ring needs neither gradient compression nor switch arithmetic and retains a startup cost that grows with rank count.
questions.learning_objective: Compare Ring AllReduce and a simple unsegmented Tree AllReduce in terms of balanced byte volume and elapsed transfer cost.

questions.question: An infrastructure engineer evaluates AllReduce algorithm selection for synchronizing gradients across a 256-GPU cluster with per-node launch latency $\alpha = 5\,\mu\text{s}$ and link bandwidth $\beta = 50\text{ GB/s}$. Using the log-aware crossover model $M_{\text{crossover}} \approx \frac{N \alpha \beta}{\log_2 N}$, within the simple full-message Tree versus Ring comparison, what is the crossover message size, and which modeled candidate has lower cost for a 500 KB activation tensor versus a 100 MB gradient bucket?
choices: The crossover is $M_{\text{crossover}} \approx 1.25\text{ GB}$; Tree AllReduce should be selected for both tensors because $\log_2(256) = 8$ is always smaller than 256.
The crossover is $M_{\text{crossover}} \approx 800\text{ KB}$; Ring AllReduce should be selected for 500 KB, and Tree AllReduce for 100 MB.
The crossover is $M_{\text{crossover}} \approx 16\text{ GB}$; Butterfly AllReduce should be selected for both tensors regardless of network topology.

The crossover is $M_{\text{crossover}} \approx \frac{256 \times (5 \times 10^{-6}\text{ s}) \times (50 \times 10^9\text{ B/s})}{8} = 8\text{ MB}$; Tree AllReduce wins for the 500 KB tensor (latency-dominated), while Ring AllReduce wins for the 100 MB bucket (bandwidth-dominated).
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. The crossover is $M_{\text{crossover}} \approx \frac{256 \times (5 \times 10^{-6}\text{ s}) \times (50 \times 10^9\text{ B/s})}{8} = 8\text{ MB}$; Tree AllReduce wins for the 500 KB tensor (latency-dominated), while Ring AllReduce wins for the 100 MB bucket (bandwidth-dominated). Equating $T_{\text{ring}} = 2(N-1)\alpha + 2\frac{N-1}{N}\frac{M}{\beta}$ and $T_{\text{tree}} = 2\log_2 N \cdot \alpha + 2\log_2 N \cdot \frac{M}{\beta}$ yields the crossover threshold $M_{\text{crossover}} \approx \frac{N \alpha \beta}{\log_2 N}$. For $N=256$, $\log_2(256) = 8$, so $M_{\text{crossover}} \approx \frac{256 \times 5\,\mu\text{s} \times 50\text{ GB/s}}{8} = \frac{64\text{ MB}}{8} = 8\text{ MB}$. For the 500 KB tensor ($M < 8\text{ MB}$), latency dominates, and Tree AllReduce wins by avoiding Ring's $2(255) \times 5\,\mu\text{s} = 2.55\text{ ms}$ startup delay. For the 100 MB bucket ($M > 8\text{ MB}$), bandwidth dominates, and Ring AllReduce wins by avoiding Tree's $8\times$ bandwidth penalty. The $1.25\text{ GB}$ crossover miscalculates the formula, the $800\text{ KB}$ choice inverts algorithm assignments, and the $16\text{ GB}$ choice ignores message-size regime transitions. These are predictions for the stated two-model comparison, not a selection guarantee over optimized trees, hierarchy, or a contended runtime. Benchmark candidate collective duration and exposed step time.
questions.learning_objective: Calculate the approximate Ring-versus-simple-Tree crossover and identify lower modeled cost under stated assumptions.

questions.question: Recursive halving-doubling (Butterfly AllReduce) combines logarithmic startup rounds with bandwidth-optimal byte volume in a flat-network model. What physical placement condition can defeat that modeled advantage, and why do double-tree or hierarchical alternatives still require measurement?
questions.answer: XOR partner pairs can share a constrained fabric cut if the rank placement sends their concurrent exchanges across it. For example, pairing the two logical rank halves crosses racks only when those halves occupy different racks. Shared paths and changing chunk sizes can then erode the flat-network advantage. Complementary trees balance logical endpoint work, and hierarchy distributes work across tiers, but neither construction guarantees disjoint physical paths or sufficient port capacity. Compare achieved collective duration and exposed step time under the actual placement.
questions.learning_objective: Explain how rank placement and shared physical paths can limit Butterfly AllReduce and its alternatives.

questions.question: Explain the structural mechanism of the Double Binary Tree AllReduce algorithm that allows it to achieve near-optimal bandwidth ($\approx 2M/\beta$) while preserving logarithmic latency ($\mathcal{O}(\log N)\alpha$).
questions.answer: Double Binary Tree divides the payload between complementary logical trees so that ranks serving as interior nodes in one tree can be leaves in the other. This balances forwarding and reduction work while retaining logarithmic depth. Pipelining the halves can approach bandwidth-efficient transfer, but complementary logical roles do not guarantee that every physical link is saturated or that the mapping avoids network contention.
questions.learning_objective: Describe how Double Binary Tree AllReduce combines complementary binary trees to achieve near-optimal bandwidth with logarithmic latency.

questions.question: Sequence the execution steps of a 4-GPU Ring AllReduce ($0 \to 1 \to 2 \to 3 \to 0$) reducing a 4-chunk vector $[A, B, C, D]$: (1) each GPU forwards its fully reduced chunk around the ring for $N-1$ steps until all ranks possess the complete array, (2) rank $i$ owns a single fully aggregated chunk of the global sum, (3) each GPU partitions its local vector into $N=4$ equal chunks, (4) each GPU simultaneously sends chunk $k$ to its right neighbor and receives from its left neighbor, accumulating partial sums over $N-1$ steps.
questions.answer: The correct order is: (3) each GPU partitions its local vector into $N=4$ equal chunks, (4) each GPU simultaneously sends chunk $k$ to its right neighbor and receives from its left neighbor, accumulating partial sums over $N-1$ steps, (2) rank $i$ owns a single fully aggregated chunk of the global sum, (1) each GPU forwards its fully reduced chunk around the ring for $N-1$ steps until all ranks possess the complete array. The algorithm first partitions the tensor into $N$ equal chunks; executes $N-1$ Scatter-Reduce steps where partial sums are accumulated; establishes that each rank holds one fully reduced chunk; and finishes with $N-1$ AllGather steps circulating the reduced chunks so every rank ends with the full result.
questions.learning_objective: Order the operational phases and dataflow transitions of a Ring AllReduce collective execution.

questions.question: Under the standard balanced point-to-point model, an AllReduce with $M$ bytes per rank has a per-rank sent-volume lower bound of $2(N-1)M/N$ bytes. Meeting this bound is known as ____ optimality, which Ring AllReduce achieves.
questions.answer: bandwidth. The ring ReduceScatter and AllGather phases each send $(N-1)M/N$ bytes per rank. The rank also receives the same total volume; adding sent and received bytes would double the one-direction accounting used with link bandwidth $\beta$.
questions.learning_objective: Identify the definition and formula for bandwidth optimality in collective reductions.

questions.question: On an 8-node cluster with 8 GPUs per node, fast local NVLink, and eight independent 50 GB/s network ports per node, how can hierarchical AllReduce improve on a flat ring whose inter-node traffic is serialized through one port?
choices: Hierarchical AllReduce converts the floating-point values to 8-bit integers during the intra-node phase to save inter-node bandwidth.
Flat Ring AllReduce requires every GPU to establish an optical fiber connection directly to all 63 other GPUs in the cluster.
Local ReduceScatter creates one 125 MB shard per GPU from a 1 GB tensor; corresponding-rank AllReduces can distribute these shards across the eight ports, followed by local AllGather.
Hierarchical AllReduce executes without any inter-node network synchronization barriers.
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. Each inter-node rank receives an input shard of $M/8$, then sends $2(7/8)(M/8)$ bytes in its eight-node ring and receives the same volume. Summing over eight local ranks gives $2(7/8)M$ sent per node, not an eightfold reduction in aggregate optical bytes. Speedup comes from the declared local aggregation and independent-port mapping; a topology-aware flat implementation can change the comparison.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze hierarchical AllReduce by separating input shard size, sent volume, aggregate node traffic, and available port capacity.

questions.question: How does dimension-ordered reduction on a 3D torus network (such as Google TPU pods) optimize communication latency and link utilization compared to running a single global logical ring?
choices: It skips communication along the Z-axis by projecting all activations onto a 2D plane.
It executes axis-aligned rings in sequence, reducing startup rounds to $2[(X-1)+(Y-1)+(Z-1)]$ while trading extra full-message transfers for shorter rings.
It broadcasts full gradient tensors directly to all pod nodes simultaneously over optical circuit switches.
It routes all collective packets through a single central root TPU in the pod to minimize total wire length.
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. Sequential full-message rings along X, Y, and Z reduce startup rounds from $2(XYZ-1)$ to $2[(X-1)+(Y-1)+(Z-1)]$. Their bandwidth time is $2M[(X-1)/X+(Y-1)/Y+(Z-1)/Z]/\beta$, not the cost of one global ring. Direct-neighbor routing avoids arbitrary paths but does not eliminate other workloads' contention. Skipping an axis omits contributions; a central root recreates a bottleneck.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze how dimension-ordered reduction on torus topologies reduces latency hop complexity from multiplicative volume to additive perimeter.

questions.question: Describe the architectural principle of rail-optimized routing in multi-GPU DGX clusters, and explain the performance pathology that occurs if a job scheduler assigns process ranks without topology awareness.
questions.answer: Rail-aware placement keeps the same model shard at the same local GPU index across replicas, aligning corresponding-rank communication with GPU-to-NIC affinities. Distinct shard groups can then use distinct rails when the topology provides them. A poor mapping may concentrate traffic on a subset of NICs or cross additional fabric tiers. Alignment does not reserve bandwidth, eliminate contention, or imply a universal slowdown factor; measure the actual placement.
questions.learning_objective: Explain the mechanics of rail-optimized routing and diagnose the performance penalties caused by topology-unaware rank placement.

questions.question: True or False: On a supported aggregation path, SHARP can move intermediate reduction arithmetic from endpoints into switches, but the resulting latency and training-step benefit still depend on message size, placement, switch resources, and exposed dependencies.
questions.answer: True. Aggregation-capable switches combine contributions in the packet path, avoiding some intermediate endpoint receive-reduce-forward work. Startup, switch processing, data movement, and contention remain. The supported operation and datatype, aggregation-resource availability, and binding links determine collective benefit; independent computation and consumer readiness determine how much reaches step time. In-network reduction does not guarantee a fixed speedup for every tensor.
questions.learning_objective: Identify how in-network reduction (SHARP) offloads collective arithmetic to switch ASICs to eliminate store-and-forward GPU memory traffic.

questions.question: Sequence the three phases of Hierarchical AllReduce executed across a multi-node cluster with $G$ GPUs per node: (1) intra-node AllGather across local GPUs over NVLink to reconstruct the full globally reduced tensor, (2) inter-node AllReduce across corresponding GPU positions over InfiniBand on the $M/G$ node shards, (3) intra-node ReduceScatter across local GPUs over NVLink leaving each GPU holding $1/G$ of the partially reduced tensor.
questions.answer: The correct order is: (3) intra-node ReduceScatter across local GPUs over NVLink leaving each GPU holding $1/G$ of the partially reduced tensor, (2) inter-node AllReduce across corresponding GPU positions over InfiniBand on the $M/G$ node shards, (1) intra-node AllGather across local GPUs over NVLink to reconstruct the full globally reduced tensor. The hierarchy first exploits high-speed intra-node NVLink to reduce local data into shards; then performs the expensive inter-node exchange only on the reduced $M/G$ payload over InfiniBand; and finally redistributes the global results locally over NVLink.
questions.learning_objective: Order the three causal phases of Hierarchical AllReduce across intra-node and inter-node network tiers.

rationale.question_strategy: Open with an applied calculation MCQ on Top-k sparsification index encoding overhead, follow with a mathematical MCQ on the error feedback telescoping sum, analyze 1-bit Adam optimizer state compression in a SHORT question, test unconditional quantization speedup misconceptions in a TF question, and explain 1-bit Adam phases and residual dependencies in a SHORT question.
rationale.difficulty_progression: Realized compression accounting (index overhead) -> Mathematical error correction (error feedback) -> Optimizer co-design analysis (1-bit Adam) -> Economic payback evaluation -> Optimizer phase and residual dependency reasoning.
rationale.integration: Connects numerical representation and optimization convergence theory to physical communication payload reduction.
rationale.ranking_explanation: This section covers gradient compression algorithms and theoretical convergence preservation under bandwidth scarcity, warranting a comprehensive 5-question technical quiz.

questions.question: A distributed training team applies Top-k sparsification with $K_{\text{top}} = 0.001 \times d_{\text{grad}}$ (retaining 0.1% of elements) to FP32 gradients ($d_{\text{grad}}$ elements at 4 bytes each). Transmitting the sparse gradient requires sending both FP32 values (4 bytes) and INT32 index locations (4 bytes) for each surviving element. What is the realized compression ratio compared to the dense FP32 gradient baseline?
choices: $500\times$, because each kept element requires 8 bytes (value plus index), yielding an encoded payload of $8 \times 0.001 d_{\text{grad}} = 0.008 d_{\text{grad}}$ bytes compared to the $4 d_{\text{grad}}$ dense baseline.
$1000\times$, because index encoding overhead is completely eliminated by the network interface hardware.
$100\times$, because the error-feedback accumulator doubles the size of the transmitted index buffer.
$32\times$, because sparse tensors automatically conform to 1-bit quantization limits.
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. $500\times$, because each kept element requires 8 bytes (value plus index), yielding an encoded payload of $8 \times 0.001 d_{\text{grad}} = 0.008 d_{\text{grad}}$ bytes compared to the $4 d_{\text{grad}}$ dense baseline. While retaining 0.1% of elements suggests a $1000\times$ reduction based on element count alone, transmitting a sparse tensor across a network requires sending both the non-zero values and their coordinate indices so the receiver can reconstruct the tensor. For $K_{\text{top}}$ elements in FP32 with INT32 indices, the message size is $K_{\text{top}} \times (4 + 4) = 8 K_{\text{top}}$ bytes. The effective compression ratio is $\frac{4 d_{\text{grad}}}{8 K_{\text{top}}} = \frac{4 d_{\text{grad}}}{8 \times 0.001 d_{\text{grad}}} = \frac{4}{0.008} = 500\times$. The $1000\times$ claim ignores mandatory index metadata, the $100\times$ claim confuses local memory storage with transmitted payload, and the $32\times$ choice confuses sparsification with 1-bit quantization.
questions.learning_objective: Calculate the realized compression ratio of Top-k gradient sparsification by accounting for coordinate index encoding overhead.

questions.question: Why is the Error Feedback mechanism ($e_{t+1} = g_t + e_t - v_t$) mathematically essential when applying aggressive lossy compression (such as 1-bit SGD or Top-k sparsification) in distributed training?
choices: It dynamically recompiles CUDA backward kernels to eliminate all register spills during gradient calculation.
It converts AllReduce operations into asynchronous point-to-point transfers to bypass network switch buffers.
It forces all model weights to remain strictly positive throughout optimization.
It preserves deferred residuals, so average transmitted and original updates differ by $(e_1-e_{K+1})/K$, which vanishes if the residual grows sublinearly.
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. Error feedback carries discarded information into later updates. Summing the recurrence gives $\sum v_t=\sum g_t+e_1-e_{K+1}$. The average difference vanishes only when the residual divided by the step count tends to zero. This identity supports convergence analysis under further assumptions; it does not guarantee convergence for any compressor or workload.
questions.learning_objective: Explain the conditional cumulative-update conservation established by the error-feedback recurrence.

questions.question: How does 1-bit Adam achieve high compression ratios on optimizer state communication without suffering the severe convergence degradation of naive 1-bit SGD?
questions.answer: 1-bit Adam first runs uncompressed Adam until the second-moment estimate stabilizes, then freezes that estimate as a preconditioner and communicates compressed momentum with residual correction. This optimizer-aware design supports the method’s convergence analysis under its assumptions. The paper reports up to fivefold end-to-end communication-volume reduction while matching uncompressed Adam’s convergence speed on its evaluated workloads; that result is not a guarantee for every workload or a fivefold training speedup. Warmup, scale metadata, encoding cost, and exposed communication determine the realized benefit.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze the two-phase architecture of 1-bit Adam that separates variance stabilization from error-compensated momentum compression.

questions.question: True or False: Applying $4\times$ gradient quantization will always decrease end-to-end training step time because reducing communication payload bytes is unconditionally beneficial regardless of whether the cluster is in a compute-bound or communication-bound regime.
questions.answer: False. Reducing payload bytes can save transfer time, but encoding and decoding consume execution resources, startup costs remain, and communication already hidden behind computation offers little exposed time to remove. In a serial synchronization budget, encoding must cost less than the transfer time saved; with overlap, compare the exposed critical-path saving. Compression can also change the number of steps needed to reach the same quality target. That penalty is workload-dependent, so evaluate complete time to quality rather than assuming a fixed extra-iteration percentage.
questions.learning_objective: Evaluate why gradient compression fails to improve wall-clock time in compute-bound or low-latency communication regimes.

questions.question: Describe the two phases of 1-bit Adam and the dependency that connects each compressed momentum message to the next residual-corrected update. Does residual storage have to wait for network transmission to finish?
questions.answer: Uncompressed Adam first stabilizes the second-moment estimate, which is then frozen as a preconditioner. In the compressed phase, the current momentum and carried residual determine the compressed message and next residual. The message is communicated through the supported compressed aggregation path, and the residual must be preserved before the next update that uses it. Computing or storing that residual need not wait for transmission to finish when buffer ownership and runtime dependencies permit; the essential order is warmup before freezing and residual production before its next use.
questions.learning_objective: Explain the two phases and residual dependencies of 1-bit Adam without imposing an unnecessary transport order.

Quantitative overlap budgeting for transformer models
rationale.question_strategy: Open with an applied MCQ on bucket fusion trade-offs in PyTorch DDP, analyze exposed communication residuals in a quantitative SHORT question, probe boundary conditions in a SHORT question, and analyze bucket membership and readiness in a SHORT question.
rationale.difficulty_progression: Architectural parameter tuning (bucket fusion) -> Quantitative overlap budgeting (exposed residuals) -> Boundary condition analysis -> Readiness-based bucket assignment reasoning.
rationale.integration: Integrates backward-pass computational graph execution with asynchronous collective communication streams.
rationale.ranking_explanation: This section details the critical technique for hiding communication latency behind backward arithmetic, warranting a focused 4-question technical quiz.

questions.question: In PyTorch DistributedDataParallel (DDP), how does bucket fusion balance the trade-off between communication startup latency ($\alpha$) and the compute-communication overlap window?
choices: Grouping multiple parameter gradients into a bucket amortizes per-collective startup overhead, but the bucket must wait until all required gradients are ready, reducing the available overlap window.
Bucket fusion compresses all gradient tensors into 8-bit integers before allocating them to ring communication buffers.
Bucket fusion permanently disables all gradient hooks and forces all communication to occur after optimizer step completion.
Bucket fusion ensures that all layers in the transformer model have mathematically identical parameter counts.
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. Fusion replaces many small reductions with fewer larger ones, amortizing startup cost. Each bucket waits for its last required gradient, so a larger bucket can delay launch enough to expose communication that smaller buckets could hide. The useful size depends on readiness, tensor sizes, achieved transfer duration, and collective ordering. Measure training-step time, including the final transfer and any backlog; larger buckets do not guarantee bandwidth saturation or only a slight delay. Fusion does not itself quantize gradients or change layer dimensions.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze the trade-off between startup latency amortization and communication launch delay in DDP bucket fusion.

questions.question: In the illustrative 32-layer, 7B-parameter FP32 gradient budget, each equal layer has 875 MB of gradients. Charging nine 100 MB buckets at 3 ms each gives 27 ms of communication per layer, while backward compute takes 15 ms. Under a single serialized communication stream, calculate total backward-plus-communication time with and without overlap and explain the exposed tail.
questions.answer: Sequential execution takes $32(15+27)=1344$ ms. With overlap, the first gradient becomes ready at 15 ms, then 32 communication stages take 27 ms each: $15+32\times27=879$ ms, a 34.6 percent saving. Compute alone takes 480 ms, leaving 399 ms exposed: a 27 ms drain plus $31(27-15)=372$ ms of backlog. These values include the stated full-bucket charge for the final partial bucket.
questions.learning_objective: Calculate exposed communication residuals in pipelined training when collective transfer time exceeds layer backward computation.

questions.question: Explain the startup and drain boundaries of bucketed backpropagation that limit communication-computation overlap even when intermediate layers hide communication successfully.
questions.answer: Communication cannot start until the first backward bucket is ready, leaving an initial compute-only startup interval. That first bucket can then overlap with later backward work; its communication is not inherently exposed. At the other end, the final bucket has no later backward computation to hide behind, so the optimizer must wait for its reduction and any accumulated communication backlog.
questions.learning_objective: Identify the output-layer and input-layer boundary conditions that prevent complete communication hiding in backward pass overlap.

questions.question: Why can one late gradient delay a DDP bucket whose other gradients are ready? Explain how parameter registration order and observed backward readiness can guide bucket membership without guaranteeing an optimal overlap schedule.
questions.answer: A bucket cannot launch its reduction until all required gradients are ready, so one late gradient consumes the overlap window of the others. Reverse parameter registration order can approximate backward readiness, and some configurations rebuild buckets using observed readiness. Registration order need not match forward execution order in branched models or models with reused parameters. Grouping gradients that become ready together can help, while the runtime must preserve compatible collective order across ranks and measure the resulting step time.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze how gradient readiness and bucket membership affect DDP communication overlap.

rationale.question_strategy: Open with an architectural MCQ on GPU-specific optimizations that differentiate NCCL from general MPI/Gloo, follow with a scenario-based MCQ on the communication library selection guide, probe nccl-tests diagnostic isolation in a SHORT question, and evaluate NCCL_DEBUG functionality in a TF question.

questions.question: Which mechanisms make NCCL a useful candidate for GPU-resident collective communication on NVIDIA clusters?
choices: NCCL runs all collective communication on host CPU threads using OpenMP parallel loops.
NCCL combines supported GPUDirect paths, fused reduction and data movement, and parallel channels with topology-aware placement.
NCCL eliminates all network synchronization barriers by approximating gradient additions as stochastic random walks.
NCCL replaces InfiniBand hardware with standard TCP/IP operating system sockets.
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. NCCL optimizes GPU-resident collectives through topology-aware transfers, fused reduction kernels, and parallel channels. GPUDirect paths avoid unnecessary host-memory staging when the hardware and configuration support them. CPU-centric paths can incur extra copies; CUDA-aware MPI can also communicate GPU buffers directly, so the advantage must be evaluated against the actual backend rather than assuming all MPI stages through host memory.
questions.learning_objective: Identify NCCL mechanisms that support GPU-resident collectives and explain why achieved performance requires measurement.

questions.question: An ML engineering team is setting up distributed training across three environments: (1) local developer laptops running macOS for unit testing, (2) an HPC cluster using Slurm where legacy CPU nodes perform data preprocessing, and (3) an 8-node NVIDIA H100 cluster for large-scale model pretraining. According to the chapter library selection guide, which backend mapping is recommended?
choices: NCCL for macOS development, NCCL for CPU preprocessing, and Gloo for H100 training.
MPI for macOS development, NCCL for CPU preprocessing, and Gloo for H100 training.
Gloo for macOS development (cross-platform portability without CUDA), MPI for CPU preprocessing (mature CPU optimizations), and NCCL for H100 multi-GPU training (GPUDirect RDMA and NVLink awareness).
Gloo for all three environments because a single unified backend always outperforms specialized hardware libraries.
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. Gloo for macOS development (cross-platform portability without CUDA), MPI for CPU preprocessing (mature CPU optimizations), and NCCL for H100 multi-GPU training (GPUDirect RDMA and NVLink awareness). Gloo requires no CUDA runtime or specialized networking, making it ideal for local laptop development and CI testing across macOS, Linux, and Windows. MPI provides decades of mature CPU-level communication optimizations and native Slurm integration for CPU-only data preprocessing pipelines. NCCL is the standard specialized backend for multi-GPU NVIDIA clusters to exploit NVLink, NVSwitch, and GPUDirect RDMA. Assigning NCCL to macOS or CPU nodes is impossible because NCCL is strictly NVIDIA GPU-dependent, and using Gloo on H100 nodes sacrifices GPUDirect and NVLink saturation.
questions.learning_objective: Design a multi-environment communication runtime configuration by selecting among NCCL, Gloo, and MPI based on hardware platform and workload constraints.

questions.question: When debugging a multi-node distributed training job that runs at 50% of expected throughput, what diagnostic information does running nccl-tests provide compared to profiling the PyTorch training loop directly?
questions.answer: Running nccl-tests measures bare collective performance for the tested message sizes, rank placement, and network conditions. Healthy isolated results shift investigation toward training-specific overlap, bucket sizes, input stalls, and shared-resource contention. They do not rule out intermittent faults or congestion that occurs only during training. Reproduce the application placement and traffic pattern before excluding the fabric.
questions.learning_objective: Explain how bare collective benchmarking (`nccl-tests`) isolates physical network fabric performance from framework-level software bottlenecks.

questions.question: True or False: Setting the environment variable NCCL_DEBUG=INFO modifies the mathematical reduction operator in NCCL from floating-point summation to exact integer bitwise addition to guarantee deterministic gradient aggregation across runs.
questions.answer: False. `NCCL_DEBUG=INFO` is strictly an observability and diagnostic logging flag. It outputs runtime metadata to standard error, including detected physical hardware topology, GPU-to-NIC affinities, selected collective algorithms (e.g., Ring vs. Tree), channel counts, and communication protocols (e.g., Simple vs. LL/LL128). It does not alter the mathematical semantics, reduction operators, or numerical precision of collective operations.
questions.learning_objective: Identify the diagnostic and logging purpose of the `NCCL_DEBUG` environment variable.

questions.question: A machine learning engineer claims: 'Setting async_op=True on PyTorch collective calls guarantees that communication will be 100% hidden behind computation, eliminating communication overhead entirely.' Based on the chapter discussion of asynchronous collectives and the LogP model, why is this claim a fallacy?
choices: async_op=True is an invalid argument that causes PyTorch to raise a runtime exception on GPU clusters.
Asynchronous operations automatically disable GPUDirect RDMA and route all traffic through host CPU RAM.

A nonblocking call does not guarantee independent work, effective runtime progress, or completion before a dependent consumer needs the result; overhead, contention, and unfinished transfers can remain exposed.
Asynchronous collectives are mathematically restricted to Broadcast operations and cannot execute gradient AllReduces.
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. Returning a work handle lets the host continue, but it does not make the transfer instantaneous or guarantee overlap. Independent computation must cover the transfer interval, the runtime must make progress, and dependent consumers must wait for completion using the backend’s synchronization contract. Launch and completion overhead or shared-resource contention can reduce the benefit. A waiting consumer does not imply that every GPU resource stalls, and nonblocking execution does not inherently disable GPUDirect or restrict collectives to Broadcast.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze the fallacy that asynchronous collectives guarantee complete latency hiding using the LogP model and stream barrier semantics.

questions.question: An infrastructure team applies $T_{\mathrm{lat}}=2(N-1)\alpha$ to every intra-node AllReduce on an 8-GPU NVSwitch system without checking the selected collective algorithm. Why can that model be misleading?
choices: DGX nodes do not contain high-bandwidth interconnects and rely solely on 1 GbE management cables.
The formula describes a logical ring. NVSwitch supports other collective schedules, so the selected algorithm and message size must be checked before assuming sequential ring rounds.
Intra-node AllReduce is forbidden by the CUDA driver, which mandates that all gradient reductions take place across inter-node InfiniBand links.
Ring AllReduce cannot operate on power-of-two GPU counts.
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. A ring can run over a switched fabric, and its round-count model still applies when that algorithm is used. NVSwitch connectivity also permits other schedules and supported reduction offloads. Physical connectivity alone does not identify the runtime algorithm or guarantee constant latency; benchmark the selected collective for the intended message size.
questions.learning_objective: Identify the modeling pitfall of applying 1D Ring AllReduce formulas to full-crossbar NVSwitch intra-node fabrics.

questions.question: Explain why evaluating a new gradient compression algorithm using only 'communication time per step' or 'network compression ratio' is an engineering pitfall, and describe the metric that should be used instead.
questions.answer: Evaluating gradient compression solely by per-step communication speedup or compression ratio (e.g., $100\times$) is a pitfall because lossy compression introduces gradient noise, variance, or systematic bias into the stochastic optimization process. If compression degrades gradient quality enough that the model requires $2\times$ more training iterations or smaller learning rates to reach the target validation loss, total wall-clock training time will increase even if individual network steps are $50\%$ faster. The true engineering evaluation metric must be 'time-to-accuracy' (total wall-clock time required to reach target convergence/validation perplexity on a realistic training schedule), not time-per-step or network payload reduction alone.
questions.learning_objective: Explain why gradient compression algorithms must be evaluated on time-to-accuracy rather than microbenchmark time-per-step.

questions.question: True or False: Topology-unaware placement can concentrate collective traffic on a subset of network interfaces, reducing realized bandwidth even when nominal aggregate port capacity is unchanged.
questions.answer: True. GPU-to-NIC affinity and the mapping of corresponding model shards determine which ports and paths carry a collective. Concentrating traffic on a few interfaces can leave others underused. The penalty depends on workload and topology; rail alignment alone neither reserves bandwidth nor removes contention.
questions.learning_objective: Evaluate how topology-unaware rank assignment causes NIC contention and degrades multi-rail collective bandwidth.

questions.question: Match the three Lighthouse Archetypes to their dominant communication friction and primary optimization strategy as established in the chapter:
choices: Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3) -> Bandwidth-bound ($\beta$), optimized by Hierarchical AllReduce and Rail-routing; Archetype B (DLRM at Scale) -> Granularity-, fabric-capacity-, or skew-bound, optimized by message coalescing, topology-aware routing, and shard balancing; Archetype C (Federated MobileNet) -> Uplink-bandwidth- and availability-bound, optimized by Aggressive Quantization with Error Feedback.
Archetype A -> Latency-bound, optimized by Star Topologies; Archetype B -> Bandwidth-bound, optimized by Ring AllReduce; Archetype C -> Compute-bound, optimized by Tensor Parallelism.
Archetype A -> Contention-bound, optimized by CPU Paging; Archetype B -> Storage-bound, optimized by Checkpointing; Archetype C -> Network-bound, optimized by SHARP In-Switch Reduction.
All three archetypes face identical communication constraints and use the exact same Double Binary Tree AllReduce configuration.
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3) -> Bandwidth-bound ($\beta$), optimized by Hierarchical AllReduce and Rail-routing; Archetype B (DLRM at Scale) -> Granularity-, fabric-capacity-, or skew-bound, optimized by message coalescing, topology-aware routing, and shard balancing; Archetype C (Federated MobileNet) -> Uplink-bandwidth- and availability-bound, optimized by Aggressive Quantization with Error Feedback. Archetype A trains massive dense weights generating multi-gigabyte gradient tensors where inter-node bandwidth $\beta$ dominates, making hierarchical reductions and rail-aligned fabrics essential. Archetype B shards sparse embedding tables; fine-grained lookup exchanges, fabric capacity, and uneven shard load decide its AllToAll time, requiring coalescing, topology-aware routing, and balanced table placement. Archetype C operates over slow, intermittent device uplinks where limited uplink bandwidth and client availability dictate aggressive quantization (e.g., INT8/1-bit) with error feedback. The star topology, checkpointing, and identical-configuration choices mischaracterize the archetypes' distinct physical regimes.
questions.learning_objective: Classify the three Lighthouse Archetypes by their dominant communication bottleneck and corresponding optimization strategy.

questions.question: For a fixed global workload, explain why adding workers can increase the share of step time spent waiting for communication. What evidence is needed before calling communication the governing constraint?
questions.answer: Added workers provide more arithmetic capacity and can shrink local computation, while required global exchanges still pay startup, transfer, and coordination costs. In a fixed-payload ring model, per-rank bytes approach a constant while startup rounds grow with group size. Real layouts can change payloads, paths, overlap, and useful kernel throughput. Communication becomes governing when its required results remain exposed on the measured dependency path; aligned readiness and transfer traces establish that condition. Aggregate utilization or worker count alone does not prove it.
questions.learning_objective: Synthesize the physical scaling asymmetry between local compute and global communication in distributed ML systems.
